activities.caption: pair each term with its definition
activities.name: socBlocksMatch

config.prompt: Pair each term with its definition:

pairs.right: the unwritten rules — queue here, don't sing on the bus
the positions you hold — student, sibling, employee — each with a script of expectations
society's durable structures for passing norms and roles on: family, school, religion, media, the state
the knowledge, beliefs and practices a group shares — the informal side of the same thing

config.why: A society itself is a very large group organised into institutions and held together over time by formalised relationships — the vocabulary the rest of the lesson runs on.

activities.anchor: Choose what looks like the most private decision
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the founding demonstration
activities.name: socSuicideSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is wrong — click it:
lines: If suicide were purely individual, the national count would drift randomly.
It does not: the rate stays stable year after year and differs systematically between groups.
Durkheim named such patterns social facts.
A social fact is internal to each of us, which is why it explains individual motives so well.
Individuals come and go; the pattern persists — that is sociology's object of study.
config.correction: A social fact is external to each of us and yet constrains us — the rate is real above any individual, which is why it explains rates, not any one person's act.
config.why: External plus constraining is the definition — and the stable, patterned rate is what makes it sociology's founding object.

items: Play — one role at a time: being the doctor, being the parent
Game — every position held in mind at once
The generalized other — society's expectations as a whole
The social 'me' forms around the spontaneous 'I'
config.why: Taking the role of the other is the mechanism — the sequence runs from copying to holding society's standpoint in a single mind.

activities.caption: drag between the everyday and the official
activities.name: socControlCompare

config.prompt: Drag between the everyday and the official:

before.label: Informal
before.text: smiles, praise, sneers, gossip, exclusion — sanctions backed by shame and conscience; norms installed so early that by adulthood most policing is self-policing (the empty red light at 3 a.m.).

after.label: Formal
after.text: laws, police, courts, graded punishments — needed because informal sanction fails at scale: a city of a million people cannot run on gossip.

config.why: Both keep behaviour inside the lines the norms drew — one lives in your head, the other in the courthouse.

activities.caption: walk the two readings of the same scandal
activities.name: socAdhesiveBranch

config.root: The same public scandal, two lenses. Walk each reading:

start.text: Lens one — Durkheim's tradition. What is the public punishment doing?

choices.label: Re-drawing the boundary — the scandal clarifies where the line is

mis1.text: That is the second lens's answer — hold it. On this reading, even deviance is useful. Why?

choices.label: Because punishment is the boundary being publicly re-drawn

mis2.text: Not the lesson's answer — shared disapproval is solidarity being produced.

func.text: Reading one complete: socialisation is society's adhesive, and the scandal is the line being clarified. Switch lenses.

marx.text: Lens two — Marxists agree it is adhesive. What did they add?

choices.label: A direction: the norms transmitted are the ones that reproduce the existing class order
A guarantee that everyone benefits equally

mis3.text: That is precisely what this lens denies — the order calls the result meritocracy, and the invoice is not neutral.

end.text: Both agree on the fact; they argue about the invoice.

config.why: One reading: adhesive and boundary-redrawing. The other: the same adhesive, pointed at class reproduction.

activities.anchor: Rosenthal and Jacobson demonstrated the mechanism in 1968
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the bloomer study
activities.name: socBloomPredict

config.q: Teachers were told that randomly selected pupils were about to 'bloom'. By year's end, what had happened?
choices: Nothing measurable — the selected pupils were no different from the rest
Measurable IQ gains in exactly those pupils
The unselected pupils gained more, out of resentment
config.why: Expectation became treatment, treatment became outcome — the self-fulfilling prophecy caught in the act, and the label helped cause the behaviour it described.

activities.anchor: rule-breakers are a different kind of person
activities.caption: true or false — who offends
activities.name: socLabelJudge

statements.s: Strain can push anyone when goals and means diverge.
statements.why: Merton's gap does not check your biography first.

statements.s: A 'deviant identity' is partly manufactured by the reaction to a first act.
statements.why: Becker: the label can become the master status everyone sees first, and the self hardens to fit it.

statements.s: Whether an act becomes an identity depends on who saw it, and what they did next.
statements.why: Most people break rules at some point — the reaction decides.

statements.s: Prison populations look unlike us because offenders are a separate breed of human.
statements.why: The distance is real; the inference is not — strain and labelling both operate on ordinary people.
